soft-33.claim: The Hindustan Times reported a review of ECINET's publicly served code by Saurav Rajput, a data scientist at the civic-tech initiative Charchagram, which found an exception written into the code that can bar Electoral Registration Officers and Assistant Electoral Registration Officers in West Bengal from the View Enumeration Form Details tile on the SIR Phase II landing page and from the notice-and-hearing dashboard. The review found no such exclusion for these officers in any other state. The enumeration form page lists each form with its documents and the booth level officer's recommendation, and holds documents labelled as hearing orders. The review read only the code a browser receives before login, on 2, 6, 7 and 9 October and in code fetched on 19 October, so it cannot say whether the rule was ever used, whether the server enforces it, or when it was added. The paper could not verify the review independently.

soft-35.claim: The Wire reported three findings from Saurav Rajput's review of ECINET's code for the civic-tech initiative Charchagram, made on 2, 6, 7 and 9 October from code the site serves publicly, with no passwords and no use of ECINET's programming interfaces. soft-44.claim: The Reporters' Collective reported that the Commission's manual for processing Form 8 corrections in its software lets an Electoral Registration Officer start a correction on his or her own motion and approve it without field verification or a hearing, so that one officer can start a change, pass over the check and approve it without the voter knowing. It examined the code of the ECINET app and reported that the software let voters' details be changed without booth level officers or other officials having to upload supporting documents. It decompiled ECINET and ERONET and reported that a registration officer could skip the booth level officer's verification and approve a correction request. It also reported that the software does not require officers to keep a record of the changes they make, and that computer operators used ECINET through the officer's login. It reported that the Commission's disclosures of correction forms give only the voter's name and Assembly constituency and no EPIC number, which it said makes it nearly impossible for the public to tell whose entry was changed. The Collective downloaded 12,082 correction forms submitted across Uttar Pradesh between April and September 2026 from the Commission's portal, while the Chief Electoral Officer's own figures put the forms accepted in those months at 33.8 lakh. It said the same manual and software are used for the regular updating of the roll in every state after the SIR.

soft-45.claim: A screen recording of the Commission's officer portal seen by The Wire shows how the logical discrepancy check flagged a woman in Deganga, North 24 Parganas, born in 1977, The Wire reported. She had named her father and the portal had found him in the 2002 roll. Under the heading 'Logical Discrepancies' the portal gave a single reason, that six other electors had also named the same man as their father, and the only option on the screen was to schedule a hearing. A leader of a booth level officers' association in West Bengal told The Wire that the BLO app changed about 16 times during the revision and that the logical discrepancy system 'was done from Delhi'. The Wire reported that booth level officers were told to verify the flagged electors in person and did so, and the leader said their reports were submitted through the software and no action was taken on them. He said the then Chief Electoral Officer, Manoj Kumar Agarwal, had told the association that his office was forwarding its letters to Delhi and that 'Whatever is being done is being done from Delhi'.
